body.why: It works mainly through guided imagery and the therapist's words, beginning with a short body-scan relaxation and inviting the client to feel the imagined care in the body.

exertion.why: It is a still, guided imagery exercise that begins with a short body-scan relaxation.

arousal.why: A body-scan relaxation and images of parents who protect and soothe aim at a calm, felt sense of security, although painful childhood memories can surface.

social.why: It is usually part of individual therapy, with the therapist's voice guiding an inward experience.

structure.why: It is a named protocol built around five qualities of ideal parents and repeated across sessions, though the developers advise tailoring the imagery to each client's attachment needs.

stance.why: It deliberately builds new experiences of being cared for so that new inner models of self and others can form, rather than only observing what is there.

depth.why: It targets the early roots of insecure attachment directly, with the client imagining being a child cared for by ideal parents.

perception.why: Almost all of the work happens in vividly imagined scenes with ideal parents rather than in contact with the outside world.

guide.why: A therapist guides the imagery in every session, with recordings only for home practice, and it is best done with someone trained in both the method and trauma care.

body.why: It works mainly through inner dialogue with parts, which clients notice as feelings, thoughts or urges, more than through posture or movement.

exertion.why: Sessions are seated conversations with attention turned inward.

arousal.why: Sessions aim for calm curiosity toward parts, but witnessing hurt exiled parts can bring up intense feelings.

social.why: It is mainly a one-to-one therapy in which the client turns inward, although couple, group and online formats exist.

structure.why: It follows a recognizable sequence, from finding and unblending from a part to befriending protectors and unburdening exiles, but the path depends on which parts show up.

stance.why: It meets parts with curiosity and compassion instead of trying to get rid of them, while still aiming to help them let go of old burdens.

depth.why: It works with exiled parts that carry old pain and shame, which means witnessing their story and bringing them out of the past.

perception.why: The work happens in an inner world of parts that the client gets to know and speaks with, rather than in contact with the outside world.

guide.why: It is normally done with a trained therapist, and people with severe trauma are advised to see a licensed IFS clinician rather than rely on books or apps.

body.why: It works mainly through catching and questioning thoughts and changing behavior, using conversation and worksheets.

exertion.why: Sessions are seated conversations, with physical activity entering only through planned activities and real-life experiments.

arousal.why: Exposure deliberately raises anxiety in manageable steps and behavioral activation adds energizing activities, while thought work in session is calmer.

social.why: It is a collaborative relationship with a therapist, also offered as group courses, workbooks and online programs.

structure.why: Sessions follow a shared agenda with agreed goals, worksheets and between-session homework, often within a protocol for a specific problem.

stance.why: Its core aim is to change unhelpful thoughts and habits by testing them against evidence and trying new behaviors.

depth.why: It focuses on current problems rather than the past, reaching history mainly through the deeper beliefs behind automatic thoughts.

perception.why: Much of the work is with thoughts and predictions, which are then checked against what actually happens in real-life experiments.

guide.why: It is usually led by a trained therapist, but group, workbook and online versions let people learn it with lighter support.

body.why: It works mostly through language, metaphors and values, with short mindfulness exercises that include making room for feelings in the body.

exertion.why: Sessions are seated conversations and exercises, with committed actions carried out in daily life.

arousal.why: Mindfulness exercises settle attention, while turning toward painful feelings and taking committed action can be uncomfortable and activating.

social.why: It is delivered one to one or in groups, and also as guided or unguided self-help.

structure.why: It is organized around six named processes, but there is no standard course and sessions mix conversation, metaphors and exercises flexibly.

stance.why: It asks people to stop struggling with thoughts and feelings and make room for them, while committing to change what they do.

depth.why: It works with present thoughts, feelings and values rather than exploring the past.

perception.why: It mixes metaphors and imagined values work with present-moment awareness exercises.

guide.why: It is mostly delivered by trained clinicians, but guided and unguided self-help versions exist and show small benefits.

body.why: It works through feeling and putting into words the emotional truth behind a symptom, rather than through bodily practice.

exertion.why: Sessions are seated conversations with the therapist.

arousal.why: It deliberately brings the emotional learning behind a symptom into awareness and makes a contradicting experience vivid, so sessions can be emotionally intense.

social.why: It is done one to one and is also used with couples and families.

structure.why: It moves through a defined sequence, from finding the emotional truth behind a symptom to juxtaposition and checking that old triggers no longer evoke the reaction.

stance.why: It aims to dissolve the old emotional learning rather than manage the symptom, though it never opposes the symptom and starts by feeling the truth behind it.

depth.why: It uncovers mostly unconscious emotional learnings, formed in response to earlier experiences, that still make a symptom feel necessary.

perception.why: It works with inner emotional knowledge, felt and put into words and then set against a vivid contradicting experience, rather than with the senses.

guide.why: It relies on a skilled therapist to find the hidden emotional truth and set up the contradiction, and a registered trial was stopped because the therapy could not be delivered in a reliable and valid way.

body.why: It works entirely through the body, with stretching and tiring exercises followed by spontaneous tremors, and needs no talk about what happened.

exertion.why: The seven exercises deliberately tire the legs and hips, including a wall sit held for a few minutes, before a phase of lying down while tremors run.

arousal.why: It is meant to calm an over-activated nervous system, although the tiring exercises and the tremors themselves can feel intense.

social.why: It is learned from a provider in private sessions or groups and then practiced alone at home.

structure.why: A fixed sequence of seven exercises sets up each session, after which the tremors are allowed to run their own course.

stance.why: The exercises deliberately trigger tremors, but the person then lets them run and only softens or stops them rather than steering what happens.

depth.why: It is aimed at stress, tension and trauma but does not require talking about what happened, though strong emotions or memories can surface.

perception.why: Attention stays with the real physical sensations of stretching and tremoring rather than with imagery or story.

guide.why: Providers recommend learning it from a certified provider first, after which it is practiced alone as self-help.

body.why: It works through the felt sense, a vague bodily sense of a situation that is not yet in words, and lets words or images come from it.

exertion.why: It is quiet inner attention, often with eyes closed, with no physical effort.

arousal.why: It asks for gentle, open, non-judging attention, starting by clearing a space, though strong feelings can come up.

social.why: It is often done with a listener who reflects back what you say, a partner or a therapist, though it can also be done alone.

structure.why: Gendlin's six steps give a clear sequence, from clearing a space to receiving whatever comes, but with practice they become a loose guide rather than a fixed recipe.

stance.why: It gives open, non-judging attention to the felt sense and receives whatever comes kindly, letting a felt shift happen rather than forcing change.

depth.why: It works with the present felt sense of a current situation or problem, though turning inward can bring up painful memories.

perception.why: The felt sense is sensed directly in the body, but the work also means finding a word or image that fits it.

guide.why: It is usually learned from a book or a Focusing trainer and then done alone, with a lay listener or within therapy.

body.why: Conversations keep returning to what is felt in the body, mixing talk with felt-sense work, parts work and presence states.

exertion.why: Sessions are one-to-one conversations, sitting still.

arousal.why: The coach deliberately slows things down toward calm, open states, and one practitioner likens the process to meditating together.

social.why: It happens in one-to-one conversations in which the coach's close tracking and mirroring is part of the method.

structure.why: There is no fixed protocol: a conversation moves between parts, felt sense, presence and nondual work depending on what comes up.

stance.why: It aims at unfoldment rather than self-improvement, helping what is already felt come fully into awareness instead of trying to fix the person.

depth.why: It works with protective parts and old emotional learnings, which its founder ties to memory reconsolidation, although as coaching it refers trauma work to therapists.

perception.why: It blends inner parts work with direct, present-moment sensing of the body and of awareness itself.

guide.why: It is delivered one to one by a trained Aletheia coach, a role the school describes as a nearly four-year training path.

body.why: With no chosen object, thoughts, daydreams, sounds and body feelings are all equally allowed, so it is neither a thinking nor a body practice.

exertion.why: You sit comfortably without moving.

arousal.why: Dropping every effort to control attention trains equanimity and tends to be restful, though beginners may doze or drift into worry.

social.why: It is sitting practice done alone, sometimes guided by a recording such as a daily audio lesson.

structure.why: It has a single instruction, to drop any intention to control attention, and no object, steps or sequence.

stance.why: Its one instruction is to let whatever happens happen, even mind wandering, which makes it the most purely allowing point on the map.

depth.why: It rests with whatever arises now and does not seek out the past, though open sitting can bring up old emotions.

perception.why: Inner daydreams and outer sounds or sensations are treated alike, which puts it midway between imagination and perception.

guide.why: A short instruction is enough to start alone, although it is usually taught as one technique within a broader mindfulness practice.

body.why: It works mainly through silently repeated phrases and the warm feeling they evoke, which jhana practice then attends to directly.

exertion.why: It is practiced sitting quietly.

arousal.why: It settles the mind into warmth and, in jhana, deep calm, although the early absorptions bring strong joy and energy.

social.why: It is practiced sitting alone or on retreats, with other people present mainly as the imagined recipients of goodwill.

structure.why: It uses set phrases and a fixed widening circle from self to all beings, and jhana practice follows a mapped progression of states.

stance.why: It deliberately builds a feeling of goodwill and then absorption rather than observing whatever is there.

depth.why: It cultivates goodwill in the present and does not explore personal history, although wishing yourself well can stir up grief.

perception.why: It starts from imagined people and silently repeated phrases, and only in jhana does attention rest on the felt pleasant feeling itself.

guide.why: Loving-kindness is often self-guided or taught in short courses, but deeper jhana is usually learned on retreat with guidance from a teacher.

body.why: Body sensations are its main field of observation, through noting the breath or sweeping attention through the body, alongside feelings and thoughts.

exertion.why: You sit still throughout, steadying the mind on the breath and then observing whatever is most obvious.

arousal.why: Steady, non-reactive observation tends to calm, although intensive retreats can bring up fear, anxiety or panic.

social.why: Daily sitting is done alone and retreats are held in silence, so other people are present but not interacted with.

structure.why: It uses specific techniques, such as Mahasi noting or the Goenka body sweep, and retreats follow a set plan, such as three days of breath awareness before body sweeping.

stance.why: It observes sensations, feelings and thoughts without reacting to them, seeking insight rather than trying to change them.

depth.why: It watches each experience arise and pass moment by moment and does not explore personal history.

perception.why: It trains close, direct observation of sensations, sounds and mental events as they arise and pass away.

guide.why: It is usually learned on courses or retreats with teachers and then kept up as daily sitting alone.

body.why: It works entirely through hard physical effort on a bike, a track, a rowing machine or with body-weight moves.

exertion.why: Each hard bout takes you close to your limit, breathing hard and barely able to talk or flat out in sprint versions, the most strenuous effort on the map.

arousal.why: Hard bouts drive heart rate and breathing close to their peak, so that talking becomes difficult.

social.why: It can be done alone with an interval timer app, and many people follow a class or a coach.

structure.why: Sessions follow precise work and rest intervals, such as 4 bouts of 4 minutes or 10 bouts of 1 minute, often run by a timer.

stance.why: It deliberately pushes the body near its limit to change fitness and mood, rather than letting experience be.

depth.why: It is entirely about present effort and does not involve personal history.

perception.why: Attention is pulled to direct physical signals, such as heavy breathing, effort and the interval timer, leaving little room for imagery.

guide.why: Most people can do it alone or follow a class, coach or app, with medical advice and supervision recommended for people with heart problems.

body.why: It works through running, throwing and catching, with tactics, calls and social talk adding a mental side.

exertion.why: Ultimate is a fast running game of repeated sprints, cuts and jumps, broken by pauses after scores and calls.

arousal.why: Sprints, friendly competition and the shared excitement of play make it strongly energizing.

social.why: Two teams play together, settle their own calls by talking them through, and often finish in a shared spirit circle.

structure.why: Games have clear rules, roles and warm-up drills, but the play itself is fast and improvised.

stance.why: It is played for enjoyment rather than to work on oneself, although regular play builds fitness, skills and friendships.

depth.why: Play is absorbed in the present game and does not involve personal history.

perception.why: Players constantly track the disc, teammates, opponents and open space on the field.

guide.why: Anyone can join a club, league or pickup game, and because Ultimate is self-officiated no referee or professional is needed.

body.why: It works through continuous rhythmic movement of the whole body, such as running, cycling, swimming or rowing.

exertion.why: It holds a steady effort for 20 to 60 minutes at a pace where you can still speak in short sentences, usually moderate to vigorous.

arousal.why: It keeps heart rate raised for a sustained period, and in one trial a 45-minute run raised euphoria while also easing anxiety.

social.why: People run alone, with a friend or in a club, and the activity itself does not depend on others.

structure.why: Its method is simple, a steady pace for a set time with gradual increases, without the precise sets or intervals of strength training or HIIT.

stance.why: It sets out to build fitness and lift mood through regular training, while the steady pace asks you to settle into the effort.

depth.why: It is about present effort and routine, not personal history.

perception.why: On a steady run of 20 to 60 minutes, outdoors or on a treadmill, attention moves between pace, breathing and surroundings, with room for the mind to drift.

guide.why: Anyone can start alone with walk-run intervals, and clubs, coaches and group running therapy are optional.

body.why: It works through muscles moving against a load, with attention on technique through a full range of motion.

exertion.why: Each set should feel hard by the last few repetitions and heavy loads build the most strength, with a minute or two of rest between sets.

arousal.why: Hard sets briefly raise effort and blood pressure, but the aim is stronger muscles rather than keeping the heart rate up, and rests come between sets.

social.why: It can be done alone, with a coach or in a class, and is mostly a solo activity.

structure.why: Sessions are built from set exercises, sets of about 6 to 15 repetitions, planned rests and progressive overload.

stance.why: Progressive overload deliberately changes the body, adding weight or repetitions as it adapts.

depth.why: It is about present effort and progress and does not involve personal history.

perception.why: Attention is on the real load, the body's position and good technique rather than on imagery.

guide.why: It needs little space or equipment and can be done alone, though beginners benefit from instruction in technique.

body.why: It mixes talk with physical contact, such as sitting with, stroking or playing with a calm dog, or working with a horse in therapy or horsemanship sessions.

exertion.why: Most sessions are physically light, such as sitting with or stroking a dog, the animal used in about 7 of 10 programs.

arousal.why: A calm, friendly animal is thought to comfort through body contact and to ease stress and anxious feelings.

social.why: Sessions bring together a professional, often a handler and a trained animal whose companionship is thought to be an active ingredient, and horse-based work points to bonding and peer support.

structure.why: It is planned and goal-directed with progress tracked, though what happens with the animal in each moment is unscripted.

stance.why: It works toward goals set in advance, such as easing anxiety or building trust, mainly through the comfort and companionship of a calm animal rather than by pushing for change.

depth.why: It works toward present goals such as easing anxiety, building trust or practicing social skills, although you may talk through something hard while stroking a dog.

perception.why: The work rests on direct, physical contact with an animal, usually a live dog or horse, in the moment.

guide.why: Animal-assisted therapy is directed by a health, education or human-service professional with a trained animal team, and lighter visiting programs are not a substitute for it.

body.why: It works through posture, slow movement and breathing, with attention resting on the body.

exertion.why: It is gentle, low-impact exercise: slow forms such as Baduanjin, or still standing and seated postures.

arousal.why: Slow movement, slow breathing and meditative attention are thought to shift the nervous system toward rest, and some trials report lower heart rate and blood pressure.

social.why: It is usually learned in a group class and then practiced at home, alone or in a group.

structure.why: Most sessions follow a set sequence of simple, repeated movements, such as the eight movements of Baduanjin.

stance.why: It deliberately regulates body, breath and mind, which Chinese medicine describes as cultivating and balancing qi, but with gentle effort.

depth.why: It works with the present body and breath and does not explore personal history.

perception.why: Attention rests on the body and the breath as you move or hold a posture, so it works with direct sensation rather than imagery or story.

guide.why: It is usually learned from a trained instructor in a group class and then practiced at home.

body.why: It works mainly through conversation and shared activity rather than through attention to the body.

exertion.why: Typical contact, such as calls, meals and chats, is physically light, though some groups are active.

arousal.why: Conversation, laughter and meeting new people raise activation, and for anxious people social situations can feel very activating.

social.why: Contact with other people is the whole practice.

structure.why: It has no fixed steps beyond putting standing dates in the calendar and following up with people.

stance.why: It deliberately changes habits of withdrawal, such as saying yes more often and testing gloomy predictions, while the time with people is simply lived.

depth.why: It is about present relationships and routines rather than exploring the past.

perception.why: It happens in direct contact with real people and places, although conversation is also full of stories.

guide.why: Anyone can do it without a professional, though in some countries a social prescribing link worker can help people find groups.

body.why: It works through walking and the senses, with attention drifting to sights, sounds and smells, while leaving room to think.

exertion.why: It ranges from a gentle park stroll to hours of steady effort on a hike, so a typical outing is light to moderate.

arousal.why: Natural settings are thought to calm body and mood and to hold attention gently, as stress reduction and attention restoration theories describe.

social.why: People walk alone, with friends or with a walking group, and walking with others adds social contact.

structure.why: There are no set steps: you choose a place or route and let the walk unfold, with forest bathing adding a loose focus on each sense.

stance.why: It lets natural settings hold attention gently so that tired attention can recover, rather than working to change thoughts or feelings.

depth.why: It stays with the present walk and its surroundings rather than exploring personal history.

perception.why: Attention drifts to what you see, hear and smell outdoors, and forest bathing uses each of the senses on purpose.

guide.why: Anyone can walk alone or with friends, and walking groups and referred nature programs are optional.

body.why: It works through raw sensory experience, such as the body scan, touch and taste, rather than through thoughts about it.

exertion.why: It is done sitting or lying still, as in the body scan, or while eating or listening with full attention.

arousal.why: It is used to settle and come back to the present, interrupting worry and rumination by attending to what can be sensed now.

social.why: It is mostly practiced alone, though MBSR teaches it in weekly group classes.

structure.why: It uses short set exercises, such as the body scan, the raisin exercise or mindful listening, inside an open and curious attitude.

stance.why: It gives open, non-judging attention to sensation rather than trying to change it, although it is often used on purpose to settle.

depth.why: It anchors attention in the present moment, deliberately away from thoughts about the past and future.

perception.why: Its whole method is direct contact with what you see, hear, touch, taste, smell and feel right now.

guide.why: Single exercises can be practiced on your own at any time, and formal courses such as MBSR are optional.

body.why: It works through sound, rhythm and movement as well as lyrics and talking about what came up.

exertion.why: Most uses, such as listening, singing or playing simple instruments, are physically light, with more effort only when moving to the music.

arousal.why: Music can shift arousal either way, but its best-studied effect is lowering physical signs of stress, such as heart rate, and felt stress, so on balance it leans calming.

social.why: It ranges from listening alone to choirs, bands and group music therapy.

structure.why: Sessions mix structured songs and listening programs with open improvisation.

stance.why: People often listen on purpose to relax or ease anxiety, while improvising and receptive listening make room to express and explore whatever feelings arise.

depth.why: It works with the feelings that music stirs, which music therapy and Guided Imagery and Music explore, rather than deliberately reaching into the past.

perception.why: It rests on hearing real sound but also invites inner images and feelings, most deliberately in Guided Imagery and Music.

guide.why: Formal music therapy needs a credentialed therapist, but most everyday uses, such as listening, singing or playing, are self-led.
